newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Muted resentment in Burundi city from summit.
newsitem.headline: Muted resentment in Burundi city from summit.

text.p: The leader of Burundi's main Tutsi party on Sunday said they opposed holding talks with Hutu rebels despite an ultimatum by regional African leaders that negotiations must start within a month.

The capital Bujumbura, populated mainly by Tutsis, was calm despite resentment that Saturday's regional summit maintained economic sanctions and gave military leader Pierre Buyoya a deadline to start talks with Leonard Nyangoma and other Hutu rebel leaders.
"This is foolishness. There is no chance that there will be negotiations with Nyangoma," Charles Mukasi, the chairman of the Uprona, told reporters.
In its only statement so far, the regime said on Saturday night the summit's decisions gravely compromised peace and showed that some regional leaders had a secret agenda.
"They have taken sides. These sanctions are not neutral because they favour the extremists," Cooperation Minister Leonidas Havyarimana told reporters.

Buyoya, installed in a July 25 army coup, was not invited to the summit but had lobbied hard for sanctions to be eased. He says the trade and transport embargo is hurting ordinary Burundians and could lead to a "radicalisation".
"To be able to negotiate you have to be alive," Havyarimana said.
A senior official of the mainstream Hutu party, Frodebu, said the decision to keep sanctions was no surprise.
Augustin Nzojiewahi told reporters Buyoya had to restore the constitution and start peace talks before sanctions imposed on July 31 were eased or lifted.
